verdicts.quote: AGS Health runs 500+ in-house digital agents and Omega has deployed 20+ Microsoft AI solutions
verdicts.explanation: AGS Health does market a "digital workforce": it announced agentic digital workforce solutions on October 13, 2025 (HIT Consultant) and launched its InnovationWorks AI center of excellence June 8, 2026, and its AI Platform materials reference digital workers. However, no reachable public source (AGS Health's website and press releases, the Oct 2025 launch coverage, or trade press) states a count of 500+ in-house digital agents/bots; AGS's homepage cites human-workforce stats (4,700+ coders, 5,500+ A/R specialists) but no bot count. The figure may come from analyst material (e.g., Everest Group profiles) or company collateral not publicly accessible, so it cannot be confirmed or refuted. (The Omega half of the sentence — 20+ Microsoft AI solutions — is confirmed; see line 354 verdict.)

verdicts.quote: Anthropic offers a BAA and zero-retention options
verdicts.explanation: Anthropic's support center documents both: "Business Associate Agreements (BAA) for Commercial Customers" and "Covered Models under a Business Associate Agreement (BAA)" describe BAA availability for API/commercial customers (BAA coverage requires signing the BAA and using eligible services/covered models); "HIPAA-ready Enterprise plans" describes HIPAA-ready offerings (with some features requiring zero data retention enabled); and the Public Sector FAQs describe zero data retention as "Anthropic does not store your inputs or outputs." Anthropic's API docs likewise reference organizations configured for zero data retention (e.g., certain models are unavailable under ZDR), confirming ZDR is an offered configuration for API customers.

verdicts.quote: software vs outsourcing breakdown past ~50 locations
verdicts.explanation: The cited Ventus.ai blog post exists at the referenced URL and states verbatim: 'As DSOs scale past 50 locations, outsourced billing breaks down. See why AI-powered dental RCM software beats BPO vendors on cost, speed, and control.' The article extensively compares dental RCM software vs outsourced billing and positions ~50 locations as the inflection point where outsourcing economics fail (percentage-of-collections fees scale with revenue rather than efficiency, plus control/data-fragmentation issues). The report's attribution 'per Ventus' is accurate. Caveat: Ventus sells AI dental RCM software, so the 50-location threshold is a vendor marketing claim, not independent research — the report cites it appropriately as Ventus's own framing.

verdicts.quote: Kaiser sues liability insurers over a \$556M MA settlement
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed by multiple sources. Kaiser Foundation Health Plan and its Colorado affiliate filed suit on Feb 20, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against nine liability insurers (AIG, Chubb, Berkley, Starr, National Fire, RSUI, Markel, Fair American, Allianz) for breach of contract, seeking up to $95M in layered D&O coverage after the insurers refused to cover any portion of Kaiser's $556M settlement (AIG paid only ~$1M in defense costs). The underlying settlement is real: DOJ announced on Jan 14, 2026 that Kaiser Permanente affiliates would pay $556M to resolve False Claims Act allegations of submitting invalid diagnosis codes for Medicare Advantage enrollees (2009-2018; ~500,000 added diagnoses; ~$95M to whistleblowers) — the largest MA fraud settlement to date per KFF Health News. The Becker's Payer Issues article exists at the exact URL cited in the report (it returns 403 to automated fetchers but appears in search indexes with matching snippet 'suing nine liability insurers for breach of contract... refused to cover any portion of its $556 million settlement... Filed February 20', and Becker's Hospital Review carries the same story).

verdicts.quote: CO-197 / CO-15 | Prior authorization/referral absent or invalid
verdicts.explanation: X12's official CARC registry defines code 197 as "Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent" and code 15 as "The authorization number is missing, invalid, or does not apply to the billed services or provider." Both are the standard prior-authorization denial codes, commonly reported with group code CO. Minor nuance: referral-specific denials are sometimes coded 183/184, but payers widely use 197 for referral/precert requirements as well, so the characterization is fair.

verdicts.quote: CO-50 / CO-55 | Not medically necessary / experimental
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 50 as "These are non-covered services because this is not deemed a 'medical necessity' by the payer" and code 55 as "Procedure/treatment/drug is deemed experimental/investigational by the payer." Exactly matches the claim.

verdicts.quote: CO-97 | Service bundled into another paid service (NCCI edit)
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 97 as "The benefit for this service is included in the payment/allowance for another service/procedure that has already been adjudicated" — i.e., bundling, the code typically triggered by NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits. Appealing/rebilling with modifier 25 (significant separately identifiable E/M) or 59 (distinct procedural service) is the standard NCCI-bypass mechanism when documentation supports it.

verdicts.quote: CO-45 | Charge exceeds fee-schedule allowed amount
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 45 as "Charge exceeds fee schedule/maximum allowable or contracted/legislated fee arrangement." With group code CO this is the routine contractual-adjustment (write-off to allowed amount) code.

verdicts.quote: CO-22 / CO-109 | Coordination-of-benefits / wrong payer
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 22 as "This care may be covered by another payer per coordination of benefits" and code 109 as "Claim/service not covered by this payer/contractor. You must send the claim/service to the correct payer/contractor." Matches the claim exactly.

verdicts.quote: CO-29 | Timely-filing limit exceeded
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 29 as "The time limit for filing has expired." With group code CO the amount is provider liability and cannot be billed to the patient, so it is typically a hard write-off unless the provider can prove timely submission on appeal.

verdicts.quote: CO-18 | Duplicate claim
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 18 as "Exact duplicate claim/service." Minor technical note: X12's own usage note says code 18 should be reported with group code OA (except where state workers' comp rules require CO), though payer remits and industry literature ubiquitously refer to it as CO-18. The substance of the claim — code 18 = duplicate claim/service — is confirmed.

verdicts.quote: PR-1 / PR-2 / PR-3 | Deductible / coinsurance / copay
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 1 as "Deductible Amount," code 2 as "Coinsurance Amount," and code 3 as "Co-payment Amount." These are reported with group code PR (Patient Responsibility), exactly as claimed.

verdicts.quote: PR-204 / CO-96 | Non-covered service/benefit
verdicts.explanation: X12 defines code 204 as "This service/equipment/drug is not covered under the patient's current benefit plan" (X12 directs it be used with group code PR, matching PR-204) and code 96 as "Non-covered charge(s)" (reported as CO-96 or PR-96 depending on liability). Both are the standard non-covered-benefit denial codes as claimed.

verdicts.quote: Payment = (Base Units + Time Units + Modifying Units) × payer Conversion Factor
verdicts.explanation: This is the standard ASA anesthesia payment formula. The American Society of Anesthesiologists' payment-basics series states payment is determined by adding base units to time units (plus any allowed modifying units for physical status and qualifying circumstances) and multiplying by a payer-specific conversion factor — unlike flat fee-schedule pricing for other CPT codes. Cross-checked with an independent 2026 anesthesia billing reference giving Payment = (B + T + M) × CF with a payer-specific CF (Medicare ~$20/unit vs commercial roughly $65–$120+/unit). One caveat worth knowing but not affecting the verdict: Medicare itself pays only (base + time) × CF and does not allow additional units for physical-status modifiers or qualifying circumstances; modifying units are recognized mainly by commercial payers per contract.

verdicts.quote: HECVAT is a higher-ed framework and is not used here
verdicts.explanation: HECVAT (Higher Education Community Vendor Assessment Toolkit) was created by EDUCAUSE, Internet2, and REN-ISAC specifically for colleges and universities to assess cloud/vendor risk. It is a higher-education-sector instrument; healthcare TPRM instead runs on SIG/CAIQ questionnaires, HITRUST, and exchanges like Censinet. (EDUCAUSE's own page returns 403 to automated fetches, but the EDUCAUSE and REN-ISAC descriptions confirm the higher-ed scope.)

verdicts.quote: (HFMA target 3–5 days)
verdicts.explanation: HFMA does not publish an official '3-5 day' DNFB target. A PwC revenue-cycle deck hosted on hfma.org (citing the HFMA MAP Key category 'Revenue Integrity') states DNFB 'should be 3-4 days of gross revenue' and lists the DNFB KPI as 4 days; in that same document, '3-5 days' is the best-practice range for the bill hold/suspense days (the lag between discharge and final bill), not DNFB. Other HFMA-MAP-derived sources cite a 5-7 day best-practice DNFB range. HFMA MAP Keys define DNFB as a tracked metric rather than a single fixed target.
verdicts.correction: Per HFMA MAP Key-based materials (PwC 'Revenue Cycle Management and Revenue Calculations,' Oct 2022, hosted on hfma.org), the DNFB benchmark is ~3-4 days of gross revenue (KPI = 4 days); the 3-5-day figure is the best-practice bill-hold period, not the DNFB target. Suggested wording: 'DNFB: revenue stuck pre-submission (benchmark ~3-4 days of gross revenue per HFMA MAP Key materials).'

verdicts.quote: total U.S. healthcare waste ~25% (\$760B–\$935B/yr)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed against the study abstract: Shrank WH, Rogstad TL, Parekh N, 'Waste in the US Health Care System: Estimated Costs and Potential for Savings,' JAMA, Oct 7 2019 — estimated total annual costs of waste were $760 billion to $935 billion, approximately 25% of total health care spending.

verdicts.quote: administrative complexity ~\$266B/yr
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed: the same JAMA 2019 study estimated administrative complexity as the largest waste category at $265.6 billion annually, which rounds to ~$266B. The study also noted no interventions were identified targeting this category.

verdicts.quote: climbed from ~\$210B (2009) to ~\$265B a decade later
verdicts.explanation: The cited Experian Health blog page states exactly this: 'In 2009, claims processing accounted for around $210 billion in wasted healthcare dollars in the US' and 'A decade later, the bill had climbed to $265 billion.' Minor note: Experian attributes the underlying figures to a CNBC report from October 2019, so Experian is the intermediary source, but the report's citation matches the page that carries the claim.

verdicts.quote: independent physician practices fell from ~60% (2012) to ~42% (2024)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed on AMA's Physician Practice Benchmark Survey page and the 2024 Policy Research Perspectives report: 60.1% of physicians worked in private (wholly physician-owned) practices in 2012 vs 42.2% in 2024 — an 18-percentage-point decline. The ~60% and ~42% roundings are accurate. (The report's footnote [17] links an AMA advocacy page rather than the benchmark survey itself, but the underlying AMA data confirms the numbers.)

verdicts.quote: averaged \$9.77M (2024), eased to \$7.42M (2025)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed by two independent sources: IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2024 put the average healthcare breach cost at $9.77M (TechTarget: 'fell by 10.6% in 2024, resting at $9.77 million'), and the 2025 edition put it at $7.42M (HIPAA Journal, TechTarget, IBM's own site), healthcare remaining the costliest industry for the 14th consecutive year. As of 2026-07-19, IBM's 2026 edition has not yet been released (IBM historically publishes in late July), so the 2025 figure remains current. Note: the $9.36M figure that also appears in HIPAA Journal's article is IBM's 2024 US all-industry average, not the healthcare figure.

verdicts.quote: ransomware attacks rose ~30% in 2025
verdicts.explanation: The cited Comparitech Q1-Q3 2025 roundup says attacks on healthcare *businesses* (third-party vendors/business associates) rose 30% year-over-year, while attacks on healthcare *providers* were roughly flat — so applying ~30% to healthcare ransomware overall overstates it. Comparitech's full-year 2025 roundup (published Jan 27, 2026, before the report was written) shows: providers 445 attacks in 2025 vs 437 in 2024 (+2%); healthcare businesses 191 vs 153 (+25%); total ~636 vs ~590 (+8%). The 'shift toward third-party vendors' part is confirmed by both Comparitech articles.
verdicts.correction: Per Comparitech's full-year 2025 roundup (Jan 27, 2026): ransomware attacks on healthcare *businesses* (third-party vendors) rose ~25% in 2025 (191 vs 153 in 2024) while attacks on healthcare providers were roughly flat (+2%, 445 vs 437), i.e., total healthcare-sector attacks rose ~8% — with the growth concentrated in third-party vendors, confirming the shift in targeting.

verdicts.quote: HECVAT is a higher-education framework
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed: HECVAT is the Higher Education Community Vendor Assessment Toolkit, developed by EDUCAUSE with Internet2 and REN-ISAC for college/university vendor risk assessment. It is not a standard instrument in healthcare vendor procurement, which relies on SIG/CAIQ, HITRUST, and platforms like Censinet.

verdicts.quote: paid-pilot-to-annual-contract conversion (60–90%+)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed against the cited SaaStr article (Jason Lemkin): paid-pilot-to-annual-contract 'conversions vary fairly widely from about 60% to over 90%,' with EchoSign converting 'well over 90%' when customers reached full production during the pilot. Minor note: that article gives the 60–90%+ range for paid pilots but does not explicitly quantify free-pilot conversion rates for comparison; the '(60–90%+)' figure as quoted in the report is accurate.

verdicts.quote: Leader in the Everest Group RCM Operations PEAK Matrix 2024
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed: Omega Healthcare's newsroom carries a press release dated December 11, 2024 titled 'Omega Healthcare Named a Leader in the Everest Group Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) Operations PEAK Matrix Assessment, 2024' (it was also a Leader in the 2023 assessment). However, a newer assessment has since been released: on June 17, 2026 Omega was named a Leader and the only Star Performer in the Everest Group RCM Intelligent Operations PEAK Matrix Assessment (2026).
verdicts.correction: Omega Healthcare was named a Leader in the Everest Group RCM Operations PEAK Matrix Assessment 2024 (announced Dec 11, 2024) and, as of June 17, 2026, was named a Leader and the only Star Performer in the Everest Group RCM Intelligent Operations PEAK Matrix Assessment 2026 — the more current credential.

verdicts.quote: 4x revenue growth, NRR >130%
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed by Adonis's own Series C announcement (March 25, 2026, $40M led by Quadrille Capital): Adonis 'achieved more than 4x revenue growth in 2025 and net retention above 130%.' Both figures match the report exactly.

verdicts.quote: 100M+ call-minutes; knowledge graph from 4M+ calls; ~50% ROI vs manual
verdicts.explanation: These figures were accurate when written but Infinitus's current stats are roughly double. The 'knowledge graph from over 4 million calls and counting' wording comes from the October 23, 2024 $51.5M Series C press release. As of July 2026, infinitus.ai states '>200M minutes of conversation automated,' '8M+ calls completed supporting +125,000 providers,' and '50% typical ROI and 10% greater data accuracy delivered.' The ~50% ROI figure remains current.
verdicts.correction: As of July 2026, Infinitus reports more than 200M minutes of conversation automated and 8M+ calls completed (supporting 125,000+ providers), with '50% typical ROI'; the 'knowledge graph built from 4M+ calls' figure dates to its October 2024 Series C announcement.

verdicts.quote: Cair Health (YC S23)
verdicts.explanation: Y Combinator's company profile confirms Cair Health is a Summer 2023 batch company building AI agents for RCM, and states it empowers 'billing companies, care management platforms, EHRs, offshore BPOs, provider groups, and specialty pharmacies,' serving 100+ practices including major billing companies and BPOs.

verdicts.quote: Stedi eliminates production minimum
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. Stedi's pricing page states: 'Stedi is pay-as-you-go. There is no monthly minimum, no per-provider fees, and no per-payer fees.' Third-party coverage (RevCycleAI, June 2, 2026) confirms the change: Stedi 'eliminated the monthly minimum for production API access,' which previously 'required a $500 monthly minimum to access production-grade API and SFTP connectivity'; accounts now start with a $100 balance and pay nothing in zero-transaction months.

verdicts.quote: 3,400+ medical and dental payers
verdicts.explanation: Matches Stedi's own marketing: the homepage says 'Connect to virtually every U.S. healthcare payer – over 3,400' (covering Medicare, Medicaid, medical, and dental), and Stedi's payer network page lists 3,676 total payers as of July 19, 2026. Note the 'broadest clearinghouse coverage' framing is the report's/Stedi's characterization ('virtually every U.S. healthcare payer'); competing clearinghouses count payer connections differently, so that superlative is contestable, but the 3,400+ number itself is accurate.

verdicts.quote: 2,700+ payers, 95%+ of U.S. payers
verdicts.explanation: Both figures match Availity's own statements. Its Healthcare Connectivity page says Availity 'connects more than a million providers with more than 2,700 payers nationwide,' and its current press-release boilerplate (e.g., Business Wire, April 27, 2026) states: 'With connections to over 95% of payers, more than 3 million providers, and over 2,000 trading partners, Availity provides mission-critical connectivity.' The homepage also shows a '95' Direct Payer Connectivity stat.

verdicts.quote: Epic App Orchard rebranded as Epic Showroom (Connection Hub, Toolbox, Workshop)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. Epic retired App Orchard (launched 2016) and replaced it with Showroom, its marketplace 'to discover services and products for use with Epic' (open.epic and vendorservices.epic.com link to Showroom). Multiple integration vendors describe Showroom's current listing tiers as Connection Hub (basic listing, ~$500/year), Toolbox, and Workshop (deeper collaboration/co-development): 6B Health ('Products are categorised into tiers such as Workshop, Toolbox, and Connection Hub'), Folio3, and Nirmitee. Minor nuance: it was a program restructuring under Epic Vendor Services rather than a simple one-for-one rename, but the tier names in the report are accurate.

verdicts.quote: HIPAA compliance / BAA availability on pay-as-you-go
verdicts.explanation: Supported by Retell's own materials: its blog post 'Can I Get HIPAA-Compliant Voice AI Without an Enterprise Contract?' says Retell 'handles HIPAA compliance on pay-as-you-go plans with self-serve BAAs, PII redaction, and secure PHI handling,' and its docs state a signed BAA is required before transmitting PHI, is self-signable at click-agreements.retellai.com, and carries 'no additional fee.' Caveat worth knowing: the pricing-page comparison table lists 'HIPAA / BAA' and 'Custom BAA' under Enterprise — the Enterprise tier gets a custom-negotiated BAA, while the standard self-serve BAA is what is available on pay-as-you-go.

verdicts.quote: >\$200M recovered
verdicts.explanation: The figure is real but it is a calendar-2022 annual total, not a current or cumulative number. Ensemble's blog (May 16, 2023) states: 'In 2022, Ensemble recovered more than $200 million in underpayments for clients, of which 70% were identified beyond the variance report,' corroborated by Becker's Hospital Review (Jan 25, 2023). No more recent aggregate underpayment-recovery figure appears on Ensemble's site; its current results pages cite only client-level outcomes ($5M recovered, $13M zero-balance recoveries, $20M+ underpayments prevented).
verdicts.correction: Ensemble Health Partners reported recovering more than $200 million in payer underpayments for clients in calendar year 2022 (70% identified beyond the variance report), per its May 2023 blog and Becker's Hospital Review (Jan 25, 2023); the company has not published a newer aggregate figure.

verdicts.quote: Crowded with hundreds of Indian RCM shops and 20-year incumbents
verdicts.explanation: The characterization is consistent with industry consensus that India's RCM/medical-billing outsourcing sector is highly fragmented (large incumbents like Access Healthcare, Omega Healthcare, GeBBS, and AGS Health plus a long tail of small shops), but no authoritative count of 'hundreds' of India-based RCM firms could be confirmed. Directory sources that would give a count (Clutch's India medical-billing listing, GoodFirms) returned 403/Cloudflare blocks, and market-research pages tried did not resolve. Plausible but not confirmable with reasonable effort.

verdicts.quote: some very large billing companies (4,000–10,000 employees) operate as "body shops"
verdicts.explanation: This is an anecdotal characterization attributed to unnamed 'industry observers' with no footnote in the report. Billing/RCM firms in the 4,000–10,000-employee band do exist (and several India-based RCM firms exceed 10,000 employees), but no published source was found confirming either the 'body shop' characterization for that size band or the '~500-employee efficiency sweet spot' claim. It cannot be confirmed or refuted with reasonable effort.

verdicts.quote: independent physician practices fell from ~60% in 2012 to ~42% in 2024
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed by the AMA's Physician Practice Benchmark Survey page, which states that between 2012 and 2024 the share of physicians who work in private practices dropped 18 percentage points, from 60.1% to 42.2%. The 2024 survey (published 2025) is the latest edition, so the figures are current as of July 2026. Becker's coverage (May 30, 2025) corroborates the 42.2% figure. Minor note: the AMA metric is the share of *physicians* working in private (physician-owned) practice, not the share of practices, but the report's numbers and attribution are right.

verdicts.quote: most expensive sector for data breaches for the 14th straight year
verdicts.explanation: IBM's 2024 Cost of a Data Breach press release does say healthcare was the costliest industry 'for the 14th year in a row' ($9.77M). But IBM's 2025 report (released July 30, 2025 — before this report was written in June 2026) kept healthcare at #1 at $7.42M, extending the streak by one more year. The count arithmetic is locked by prior editions: the 2023 report marked the 13th consecutive year ($10.93M), 2024 the 14th, so 2025 is the 15th. Since the same sentence in the report cites the 2025 figure, the '14th straight year' phrasing is stale.
verdicts.correction: Healthcare has been the most expensive sector for data breaches in every IBM Cost of a Data Breach report since 2011 — the 14th year in a row as of the 2024 report, extended to a 15th consecutive year by the 2025 report (July 30, 2025), in which healthcare remained the costliest industry at $7.42 million.

verdicts.quote: healthcare breach cost was **\$9.77 million in 2024**
verdicts.explanation: The $9.77 million figure is confirmed by IBM's own 2024 press release ('healthcare participants saw the costliest breaches across industries with average breach costs reaching $9.77 million') and by HIPAA Journal. However, the report's parenthetical '(the most expensive year on record)' is false for healthcare: 2024 was a 10.6% *decline* from the healthcare record of $10.93 million in the 2023 report (IBM's 2023 release: 'nearly $11 million'); 2022 was $10.10 million. What hit a record in the 2024 report was the global all-industry average ($4.88 million), not the healthcare figure.
verdicts.correction: Per IBM's 2024 Cost of a Data Breach report, the average healthcare breach cost was $9.77 million — down 10.6% from the record $10.93 million in the 2023 report. (It was the global all-industry average, $4.88 million, that set a record in the 2024 report.)

verdicts.quote: eased to **\$7.42 million in 2025**
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed: IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report (released July 30, 2025) put the average US healthcare breach cost at $7.42 million, a $2.35 million year-over-year drop from $9.77 million, with healthcare still the costliest industry studied. As of mid-July 2026 the 2025 edition remains the latest (IBM typically releases the next edition in late July; no 2026 report was found in IBM's newsroom).

verdicts.quote: rose roughly **30% in 2025** as attackers shifted toward third-party vendors
verdicts.explanation: Matches the report's cited source (Comparitech, footnote [94]) exactly: 'Attacks on healthcare providers are similar to 2024's figures during the same period, but attacks on healthcare businesses rose by 30 percent' (Q1–Q3 2025 vs Q1–Q3 2024). Comparitech also explicitly describes the shift: providers 'now face ransomware threats from a different angle — the third-party contractors they enlist,' with US attacks on healthcare businesses up 51% (43 to 65) while direct provider attacks fell 8%. The report's scoping to 'healthcare-sector businesses, including medical-billing vendors' faithfully tracks the source; the only minor caveat is the source covers Q1–Q3 2025 rather than the full year, which 'roughly' reasonably absorbs.

verdicts.quote: an AHA survey found ~94% of hospitals using Change reported a financial impact
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed against the AHA survey document itself: '94% of hospitals report financial impact, with more than half reporting "significant or serious" impact.' The survey was fielded to all US hospitals with responses from nearly 1,000 hospitals, collected March 9–12, 2024, after the February 21, 2024 Change Healthcare cyberattack. The report's gloss 'hospitals using Change' is a fair reading (the survey measured impact of the Change outage among respondents).

verdicts.quote: about a third (33%) said more than half their revenue was affected
verdicts.explanation: The 33% figure is real but its denominator is wrong in the report. Per the AHA survey PDF: '82% of hospitals report impacts on their cash flow. Of these: More than 33% report impact to more than half of their revenue.' So the 'more than half of revenue' share applies to the subset of hospitals reporting cash-flow impacts (82% of respondents), not to all hospitals — roughly 27% of all surveyed hospitals, not 33%.
verdicts.correction: In the AHA survey (nearly 1,000 hospitals, March 9–12, 2024), 82% of hospitals reported cash-flow impacts, and of those, more than 33% reported impact to more than half of their revenue — i.e., roughly 27% of all surveyed hospitals.

verdicts.quote: ERA can run ~4 weeks
verdicts.explanation: The report itself flags this as 'observed, not a published SLA,' and that is accurate: Availity publishes no fixed timeline for per-payer ERA (835) enrollment, which varies by payer. A ~4-week figure is plausible and consistent with commonly quoted payer ERA-enrollment windows (~30 days), but no public Availity or payer documentation confirming an Availity-specific ~4-week timeframe could be reached (vendor help pages returned 403 errors). Cannot be confirmed or refuted with reasonable effort.

verdicts.quote: Base units (3–25) reflect complexity
verdicts.explanation: Base units do reflect procedural complexity, but the stated range understates the maximum. Anesthesia billing sources that track the CMS anesthesia base unit file and the ASA Relative Value Guide state base units 'are valued from 3 to 30, depending upon the procedure' (MSN Healthcare Solutions, an anesthesia billing firm comparing CMS vs ASA base unit values). The highest-valued code is CPT 00796 (anesthesia for liver transplant, recipient) at 30 base units; the minimum is 3. Web search budget was exhausted this session, so verification used direct fetches of billing-industry sources; two independent sources confirm the 3–30 range.
verdicts.correction: Anesthesia base units range from 3 to 30 (not 3 to 25) per the CMS anesthesia base unit file and the ASA Relative Value Guide, as of 2026; the top value is CPT 00796 (liver transplant recipient) at 30 base units.

verdicts.quote: time units are contract-defined (15 min/unit for some payers; Medicare prorates per minute)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. The Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Ch. 12) instructs that 'the A/B MAC computes time units by dividing reported anesthesia time by 15 minutes' and to 'round the time unit to one decimal place' — i.e., fractional units (e.g., 37 minutes = 2.5 units), not whole 15-minute blocks. Commercial payers commonly define one unit as 15 minutes by contract, with some using 10- or 12-minute increments or different rounding rules. Minor nuance: Medicare's proration is minutes/15 rounded to one decimal place rather than literally per-minute, which matches the parenthetical '(minutes/15, fractional)' in the claim.

verdicts.quote: modifiers encode physical status (P1–P6) and QK/QX/QZ medical-direction/CRNA supervision
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. Anesthesia claims use ASA physical status modifiers P1–P6 (P1 healthy through P6 brain-dead organ donor) and HCPCS medical-direction/CRNA modifiers: QK (physician medical direction of 2–4 concurrent procedures), QX (CRNA service with medical direction by a physician), QZ (CRNA service without medical direction). The full set also includes AA (personally performed), QY (medical direction of one CRNA), and AD (supervision of more than 4 concurrent procedures), but the report's examples are accurate as far as they go.

verdicts.quote: 90834 (38–52 min) vs 90837 (53+ min) turns on the CPT midpoint rule
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed against the American Psychological Association's practice/reimbursement page on psychotherapy codes, which states the CPT time-rule ranges: 90832 (30 min) = 16–37 minutes; 90834 (45 min) = 38–52 minutes; 90837 (60 min) = 53 or more minutes. The ranges derive from the CPT midpoint/time rule (a code may be reported once the midpoint between adjacent timed codes is passed).

verdicts.quote: Billing 90837 for a 50-minute session is the most-audited upcode in the specialty
verdicts.explanation: The technical core is confirmed: 50 minutes falls in the 90834 range (38–52 min), so billing 90837 (53+ min) for a 50-minute session is an upcode. Heavy audit scrutiny of 90837 is well documented — compliance sources describe 90837/90834 as sitting 'at the center of more post-payment audits, recoupment demands, and internal compliance failures than almost any other code pair in outpatient psychiatry,' and payers (e.g., Optum, Anthem historically) have sent utilization-review letters to high-90837 billers. The superlative 'most-audited upcode in the specialty' is a characterization that cannot be strictly ranked from public data, but it is a defensible, widely repeated industry claim rather than an error.

verdicts.quote: Telehealth needs modifier 95/93 with POS 02/10 or claims auto-reject
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed as a directionally accurate summary of prevailing billing rules: modifier 95 flags synchronous audio-video telehealth, modifier 93 flags audio-only, POS 02 = telehealth other than patient's home (typically paid at facility rate), POS 10 = telehealth in patient's home (non-facility rate); billing guides confirm that a missing/wrong modifier or POS code triggers denials or underpayment. Two nuances worth noting for a report: (1) requirements are payer-specific — Medicare keys primarily off POS 02/10 and requires 93/FQ for audio-only behavioral health, requiring modifier 95 only in limited scenarios; (2) since Jan 1, 2025 the AMA's new telemedicine CPT codes 98000–98016 replace modifier-based reporting for some commercial payers. 'Auto-reject' is a slight rhetorical overstatement (many payers deny rather than front-end reject), but the operational point stands.

verdicts.quote: IOP/PHP almost always need prior auth
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed for commercial coverage, which is the report's context: major commercial payers (e.g., UnitedHealthcare behavioral health prior-authorization requirement lists, BCBS Michigan clinical program requirements for behavioral-health PHP/IOP) require prior authorization for PHP and IOP levels of care, with emergency/urgent care exempt; behavioral-health operations guides (e.g., Valant) treat PA as a standard requirement when expanding into IOP/PHP. Nuance: traditional Medicare fee-for-service covers PHP (and, since 2024, IOP) under certification/plan-of-care requirements rather than prior authorization, so 'almost always' is accurate for commercial and Medicare Advantage but not Medicare FFS.

verdicts.quote: per-payer EDI/ERA enrollments, the long pole, weeks per payer
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed as a fair industry characterization. Payer-side evidence: Premera's ERA enrollment instructions say 'allow up to 4 weeks for enrollment process.' Clearinghouse evidence: Stedi's transaction-enrollment documentation notes that while many enrollments complete in 24–48 hours, some payers 'may require up to 30 days' depending on their internal processes; legacy clearinghouse ERA/EFT enrollments (especially for government payers requiring wet signatures or bank verification) routinely run 2–6 weeks. So 'weeks per payer' for the slow payers — and enrollment being the long pole in a go-live — is accurate, with the caveat that modern API-first clearinghouses complete many payers in days.

verdicts.quote: Base units (3–25) reflect complexity; time units are contract-defined (15 min/unit for some payers
verdicts.explanation: The time-unit half is correct (commercial contracts commonly define 15 minutes per unit; Medicare divides minutes by 15 and rounds to one decimal). The base-unit range is understated: billing sources tracking the CMS base unit file and ASA Relative Value Guide put the range at 3 to 30, with CPT 00796 (liver transplant recipient) at the 30-unit maximum. Same defect as the other line-299 base-unit claim.
verdicts.correction: Anesthesia base units range from 3 to 30 (top value: CPT 00796, liver transplant recipient, 30 units) per the CMS anesthesia base unit file and ASA Relative Value Guide, as of 2026; time units remain contract-defined (commonly 15 min/unit commercially, minutes/15 rounded to one decimal for Medicare).

verdicts.quote: the prudent-layperson standard and the facility-vs-professional split
verdicts.explanation: All three elements confirmed. (1) The prudent-layperson standard is federal law (BBA 1997 for Medicare/Medicaid managed care, codified at 42 CFR 438.114; extended to individual/group plans by the ACA): emergency coverage must be based on presenting symptoms as judged by a prudent layperson, not final diagnosis — ACEP maintains extensive guidance on it. (2) ED billing splits into a facility claim (UB-04/institutional) and a professional claim (CMS-1500) with separate reimbursement (e.g., 2026 Medicare Level-5 facility ~$612 vs professional ~$171 per billing references). (3) Payer algorithmic downcoding of Level 4–5 ED E/M (99284/99285) is a documented, widespread revenue issue with published payer ED claim-review policies (Cigna, UnitedHealthcare) and ACEP/AHA pushback.

verdicts.quote: Payer edits refresh quarterly
verdicts.explanation: CMS maintains the National Correct Coding Initiative (NCCI) procedure-to-procedure edit tables and MUEs and updates them on a quarterly basis (effective Jan 1, Apr 1, Jul 1, Oct 1), and commercial payer claim-edit libraries typically refresh on the same quarterly cadence following the CPT/HCPCS and NCCI cycles. Note: CMS.gov and Medicaid.gov blocked automated fetches (HTTP 403), so the quarterly cadence was confirmed via a secondary reference describing CMS's practice; the primary source is the CMS NCCI edits page.

verdicts.quote: any frontier provider with a BAA and zero-retention terms works
verdicts.explanation: Anthropic's official API data-retention docs (current as of July 2026) confirm both offerings: (1) HIPAA-ready API access with a signed BAA — eligible organizations can review and execute Anthropic's standard BAA directly in the Claude Console — and (2) zero data retention (ZDR) arrangements enabled per organization via the sales team. Minor nuances worth knowing: Anthropic positions the BAA/HIPAA-readiness arrangement (not ZDR) as the one to use for PHI ('If your organization handles PHI, HIPAA readiness is the arrangement to use; you do not also need ZDR'), some stateful features (Batches, Files API, code execution) are excluded, and the newest Covered Models (Claude Fable 5 / Mythos 5) require 30-day retention and are not available under ZDR — though the model used in the report (claude-sonnet-4-6) is fully ZDR- and HIPAA-eligible.

verdicts.quote: **pyx12** or **Stedi JSON API** | Smooks/edi-tools (JVM) | Never regex X12; validate against 5010 IGs
verdicts.explanation: All components check out: pyx12 is a Python 'HIPAA X12 document parser, validator and converter' that validates against X12 Implementation Guideline representations and ships 5010 maps (e.g., 270.5010.X279.A1.xml, generating 999 responses for 5010). Stedi offers JSON APIs for healthcare EDI — 837P/837I/837D claims and 270/271 eligibility accepted in JSON or X12, with JSON-to-X12 translation. Smooks is an open-source extensible Java (JVM) framework that handles EDI parsing/transformation. And HIPAA-mandated transaction sets use X12 version 005010 (e.g., 837 005010X222A2, 835 005010X221A1, 270/271 005010X279A1), the version mandated for HIPAA transactions since January 1, 2012.

verdicts.quote: **FHIR Financial resources** (Claim, ExplanationOfBenefit, Coverage…)
verdicts.explanation: The HL7 FHIR specification's Financial module defines exactly these resources: Claim (Billing section), ExplanationOfBenefit, and Coverage (Support/Administrative section), among others (ClaimResponse, CoverageEligibilityRequest, etc.). The X12-mapping aspect is also sound in practice: the base FHIR spec page does not itself carry formal X12 mapping tables, but the Claim/EOB resources correspond functionally to X12 837/835 content, and US implementation guides (e.g., CARIN Blue Button) define the mapping of X12 835/837-derived adjudication data into ExplanationOfBenefit.

verdicts.quote: model="claude-sonnet-4-6"
verdicts.explanation: "claude-sonnet-4-6" is a valid, active Anthropic API model identifier as of mid-2026. Anthropic's current official documentation explicitly lists 'Claude Sonnet 4.6 (claude-sonnet-4-6)' among supported models (e.g., on the adaptive thinking and effort pages), and it remains an active previous-generation Sonnet model (Claude Sonnet 5 is the newer Sonnet tier, but Sonnet 4.6 is not deprecated or retired).

verdicts.quote: thinking={"type": "adaptive"}
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed against Anthropic's official adaptive-thinking documentation: the Messages API accepts thinking={"type": "adaptive"} (no beta header required), and it is the recommended thinking mode on Claude Sonnet 4.6 — the model used in the report's code sample — as well as Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8 and Sonnet 5. The docs show the exact Python syntax `thinking={"type": "adaptive", ...}` on `client.messages.create()`.

verdicts.quote: output_config={"effort": "high"}
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed against Anthropic's official effort documentation: the Messages API accepts an output_config parameter with an "effort" field (values low/medium/high, plus xhigh and max on supported models), generally available with no beta header. The docs show the exact syntax `output_config={"effort": ...}` in Python, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (the model in the report's sample) supports it; "high" is the API default, so passing it explicitly is valid and equivalent to omitting it.

verdicts.quote: output_config={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": ...}}
verdicts.explanation: All three parts confirmed against Anthropic's official structured-outputs documentation: (1) `output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema: {...}}}` is the canonical API-level parameter on messages.create(); (2) the SDKs provide `client.messages.parse()` — Python accepts a Pydantic model (via output_format) and returns a validated `parsed_output`, TypeScript accepts Zod schemas via `zodOutputFormat()`; (3) tool definitions accept `strict: true` (with `additionalProperties: false` and `required`) to guarantee schema-valid tool inputs. Structured outputs are GA on current models.

verdicts.quote: Most payers require per-payer EDI/ERA enrollment (sometimes wet-signature) taking days to weeks each
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed by clearinghouse documentation (Stedi): ERA (835) enrollment is required by essentially all payers ('For 835 ERAs, always yes'), while claims (837) enrollment is payer-dependent (required by Medicare, Medicaid, and many BCBS plans in particular). Timelines match: 'Most enrollments are completed within 24 - 48 hours. However, some payers may take up to 30 days' — i.e., days to weeks per payer. Signature forms are also confirmed: some payers require providers to complete/sign enrollment PDF forms as part of their standard process (Stedi notes it signs enrollment PDF forms on the customer's behalf 'when possible' and flags PROVIDER_ACTION_REQUIRED otherwise); a subset of payers still require physically signed (wet-ink) forms.

verdicts.quote: Da Vinci implementation guides (PAS for prior auth)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed: the HL7 Da Vinci project publishes FHIR implementation guides for payer-provider administrative use cases, and the Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support (PAS) FHIR IG — currently v2.2.1 (STU 2), built on FHIR R4 and published by HL7 at hl7.org/fhir/us/davinci-pas — is specifically the prior-authorization guide. (Related Da Vinci prior-auth guides CRD and DTR also exist; PAS covers the authorization submission itself.)

verdicts.quote: | **278** | Prior authorization request / response |
verdicts.explanation: 45 CFR 162.1302 adopts "ASC X12 ... Health Care Services Review—Request for Review and Response (278), May 2006, ASC X12N/005010X217" as the HIPAA standard for referral certification and authorization — i.e., the prior authorization request/response transaction. Availity's HIPAA Transaction API docs likewise label 278 as "Service Reviews (278 authorizations)".

verdicts.quote: | **834** | Enrollment (employer/plan → payer) |
verdicts.explanation: 45 CFR 162.1502 adopts "ASC X12 ... Benefit Enrollment and Maintenance (834), August 2006, ASC X12N/005010X220" as the HIPAA standard for enrollment and disenrollment in a health plan; the 834 is sent by the plan sponsor (e.g., employer) to the payer.

verdicts.quote: | **820** | Premium payment |
verdicts.explanation: 45 CFR 162.1702 adopts "ASC X12 ... Payroll Deducted and Other Group Premium Payment for Insurance Products (820), February 2007, ASC X12N/005010X218" as the HIPAA standard for health plan premium payments.

verdicts.quote: Each X12 file is a nested envelope (ISA/IEA → GS/GE → ST/SE)
verdicts.explanation: Standard X12 structure: ISA/IEA are the Interchange Control Header/Trailer, GS/GE the Functional Group Header/Trailer, and ST/SE the Transaction Set Header/Trailer, nested in that order. Confirmed against Stedi's X12 segment reference (ISA "Interchange Control Header", GS "Functional Group Header", etc.).

verdicts.quote: Use a real parser (pyx12 or Stedi's JSON API in Python; Smooks/edi-tools on the JVM)
verdicts.explanation: All named tools exist: pyx12 is a "HIPAA X12 document parser, validator and converter" in Python (actively maintained, v4.0.0 released May 2026); Stedi offers JSON APIs that accept/return healthcare transactions "in either JSON or X12 EDI" (eligibility, 837P/I/D claims, ERAs); Smooks is a JVM data-integration framework with an EDI cartridge (note: its turnkey schemas target EDIFACT — X12 needs custom DFDL schemas); Ballerina edi-tools is a JVM-based (Ballerina/Java) EDI library that explicitly supports X12 schema-based parsing.

verdicts.quote: validate against the 5010 implementation guides
verdicts.explanation: As of July 2026, 45 CFR Part 162 still mandates the ASC X12N version 005010 TR3s for all HIPAA X12 transactions (005010X217 for 278, 005010X279 for 270/271, 005010X212 for 276/277, 005010X220 for 834, 005010X218 for 820, etc.), and the regulation text shows the same 005010 standards continuing even after August 14, 2027 — the 2027 transition applies to the NCPDP retail-pharmacy standard (Version F6), not the X12 5010 guides. No newer X12 version (e.g., 8020) has been adopted.

verdicts.quote: offers a REST/JSON API (OAuth 2.0) for real-time 270/271, 276/277, 278, plus SFTP batch for 837/835
verdicts.explanation: Availity's developer documentation states "All Availity REST APIs support OAuth 2.0 over HTTPS" and that the APIs "return JSON and XML representations"; its HIPAA Transaction APIs include Coverages (ASC X12N 270/271), Claim Statuses (ASC X12N 276/277), and Service Reviews (ASC X12N 278). Batch 837/835 exchange via SFTP mailboxes is confirmed by Availity's EDI Clearinghouse offering (claims submission and electronic remittance delivery) and Availity Essentials/payer EDI connection guides describing SFTP mailbox setup for batch X12 file submission.

verdicts.quote: 837 → `Claim`, 835 → `ExplanationOfBenefit`, 270/271 → `CoverageEligibilityRequest`
verdicts.explanation: Directionally right but the attribution is off in two ways. (1) The FHIR Financial Module does not publish X12 mappings — HL7's official Claim mappings are "to UB04 and CMS1500", and the X12 correspondences are informal community analogies. (2) Per the FHIR spec, the payer adjudication analog of the 835 is ClaimResponse, not ExplanationOfBenefit: the EOB page states the EOB "SHALL NOT be used as a replacement for a ClaimResponse" and is a patient-facing resource that "combines key information from a Claim, a ClaimResponse and optional Account information". Mapping 277 to ClaimResponse is likewise loose (claim status has no exact FHIR analog). The Da Vinci part is accurate — Da Vinci IGs (e.g., Prior Authorization Support/PAS, plus CRD, DTR, CDex) cover payer-provider administrative FHIR APIs.
verdicts.correction: More precise mapping (as of FHIR R4, July 2026): 837 ≈ Claim; 835 ≈ ClaimResponse (payer adjudication/remittance to the provider), while ExplanationOfBenefit is the patient-facing resource combining Claim + ClaimResponse (used, e.g., in CARIN Blue Button to expose adjudicated claims data); 270/271 ≈ CoverageEligibilityRequest/CoverageEligibilityResponse; 276/277 has no direct FHIR resource — status is conveyed via ClaimResponse/Task in Da Vinci workflows. Note these X12 analogies are informal: HL7's official Claim mappings are to UB-04/CMS-1500. Da Vinci implementation guides (PAS, CRD, DTR, CDex, PDex) do cover administrative FHIR APIs.

verdicts.quote: US-certified coders (AAPC: CPC/CIC/COC, or AHIMA: CCS/CCA/CDIP)
verdicts.explanation: All six credentials exist and are correctly attributed: AAPC offers the CPC (Certified Professional Coder), CIC (Certified Inpatient Coder), and COC (Certified Outpatient Coder); AHIMA offers the CCS (Certified Coding Specialist), CCA (Certified Coding Associate), and CDIP (Certified Documentation Integrity Practitioner). Minor nuance: CDIP is a clinical documentation integrity credential rather than a pure coding credential, but it is an AHIMA certification commonly held in coding/CDI teams.

These are the core HIPAA-adopted X12 transaction sets for RCM per 45 CFR Part 162: 837 health care claims (Subpart K), 835 health care payment/remittance advice (Subpart P), 270/271 eligibility inquiry/response (162.1202, 005010X279), 276/277 claim status request/response (162.1402, 005010X212), and 278 health care services review/prior authorization (162.1302, 005010X217).

verdicts.quote: its substrate (CARC/RARC/NCCI/CPT/ICD) is public
verdicts.explanation: Four of the five code sets are freely accessible: the CARC and RARC lists are publicly viewable on x12.org; CMS publishes NCCI edit files as free public downloads (quarterly PTP/MUE files confirmed on the CMS NCCI page); and ICD-10-CM is in the public domain, downloadable free from CDC/CMS (verified by downloading the official FY2026 file from CDC's FTP server). But CPT is not public: the AMA states 'CPT is copyrighted by the AMA and as such must be licensed to be used in electronic products or other forms' and 'Any entity using CPT content anywhere worldwide must have a license authorizing the use of CPT code set from the AMA or an authorized distributor.'
verdicts.correction: The substrate is only partly public: CARC/RARC lists are freely viewable on x12.org, NCCI edit files are free public downloads from CMS, and ICD-10-CM is in the public domain (CDC/CMS); CPT, however, is copyrighted by the AMA and any use in electronic products requires a paid AMA license (as of July 2026).

verdicts.quote: a library that has grown to roughly 72,000 codes
verdicts.explanation: I downloaded the official FY2026 ICD-10-CM code file (icd10cm-codes-2026.txt, published June 2025, effective Oct 1, 2025 — the code set in force when the report was written in June 2026) from the CDC/NCHS server and counted 74,719 valid (billable) diagnosis codes (98,186 total entries including 23,467 non-billable category/header codes). The FY2027 file released June 16, 2026 contains 74,879 valid codes. 'Roughly 72,000' matches the FY2021–FY2022 era and is about 4% low for 2026.
verdicts.correction: The ICD-10-CM code set contains 74,719 valid (billable) diagnosis codes in FY2026 (effective Oct 1, 2025), rising to 74,879 in FY2027 (released June 2026, effective Oct 1, 2026) — roughly 74,700–74,900 codes, per the official CDC/CMS code files.

verdicts.quote: **CPT/HCPCS** for procedures and services (over 10,000 codes)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. The AMA's CPT 2024 press release states: 'With 11,163 codes that describe the medical procedures and services available to patients, the CPT code set continues to grow...' — and it has grown since (CPT 2025 added 270 new codes / deleted 112; CPT 2026 made 418 changes including 288 new codes), putting CPT alone well above 11,000. HCPCS Level II (maintained by CMS for products, supplies, and services not in CPT) adds several thousand more alphanumeric codes on top. 'Over 10,000' is comfortably correct.

verdicts.quote: Roughly 95% of U.S. claims are submitted electronically
verdicts.explanation: The 2024 CAQH Index (the most recent full public report, published Feb 2025; I extracted the figures from the report PDF) shows medical claim submission electronic adoption at 98% — 'With 98 percent of medical claims submitted electronically...' — with a 97%/98%/98% fully-electronic trend over the last three measured years, and dental at 90%. So 95% understates current medical electronic claim submission by about 3 points; medical adoption has been at or above 97% since at least 2022. (A 2025 Index, now branded DataSpring powered by CAQH, exists behind registration.)
verdicts.correction: Approximately 98% of U.S. medical claims are submitted electronically (fully electronic), per the 2024 CAQH Index (published February 2025); dental claims are at 90%.

verdicts.quote: payer-specific edits that refresh quarterly
verdicts.explanation: Quarterly is the industry-standard edit refresh cadence, anchored by CMS: the NCCI PTP and MUE edit files are issued on a quarterly cycle (effective Jan 1, Apr 1, Jul 1, Oct 1 — the CMS NCCI page documents '1st Quarter, 2025', '2nd Quarter, 2025', '4th quarter of 2025' replacement files), and HCPCS Level II also updates quarterly. Commercial payers generally sync their edit libraries to these quarterly code/edit cycles, though exact timing of proprietary payer edits varies (some update monthly or ad hoc) — a reasonable generalization as written.

verdicts.quote: *Professional* (837P → CMS-1500, 33 fields)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. Professional claims are billed electronically on the X12 837P and on paper via the CMS-1500 (NUCC 02/12 version, in effect since April 1, 2014). I downloaded the official NUCC 1500 claim form PDF and verified the numbered items run from 1 through 33, ending with '32. SERVICE FACILITY LOCATION INFORMATION / 33. BILLING PROVIDER INFO & PH #' (some items have lettered sub-fields like 32a/33b, but the standard characterization is 33 items).

verdicts.quote: 837I → UB-04/CMS-1450, 81 "Form Locators"
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. Institutional claims use the X12 837I electronically and the UB-04 (CMS-1450) on paper. I checked CMS's Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 25 ('Completing and Processing the Form CMS-1450 Data Set'), which maps the form's Form Locators — the numbering runs through FL81 (FL76 Attending Provider, FL77 Operating Physician, etc., with FL81 as the final code-code field), i.e., 81 Form Locators.

verdicts.quote: coder certification (CPC vs CIC/CCS)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. AAPC's CPC (Certified Professional Coder) page states the credential 'validates a professional's comprehensive knowledge of medical coding across outpatient and physician services' — i.e., professional-fee coding. AAPC's CIC is explicitly the 'Certified Inpatient Coder — Hospital Coding' credential, and AHIMA's CCS (Certified Coding Specialist) is the mastery-level credential for coding inpatient (and outpatient) hospital records. Minor nuance: CCS covers both inpatient and outpatient facility records, but it is indeed the standard hospital-side credential, so the contrast as written is accurate.

verdicts.quote: Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (CARC) and Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARC) on the 835
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed on X12's official code list pages. CARCs communicate why a claim or service line was paid differently than billed, and X12 states 'Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARCs) are used to provide additional explanation for an adjustment already described by a Claim Adjustment Reason Code (CARC) or to convey information about remittance processing.' Both code lists are used in the X12 835 remittance advice (CARC 16's own text references 'the 835 Healthcare Policy Identification Segment (loop 2110 Service Payment Information REF)').

verdicts.quote: CO-16 | Missing/incomplete information (member ID, NPI, modifier)
verdicts.explanation: Confirmed. X12's official CARC list defines code 16 as 'Claim/service lacks information or has submission/billing error(s),' with the usage note that at least one Remark Code (RARC or NCPDP Reject Reason Code) must accompany it to identify the specific missing/invalid element — consistent with the report's examples (member ID, NPI, modifier). Paired with group code CO (Contractual Obligation) it appears as CO-16, and because the fix is supplying the missing/corrected information and resubmitting, it is conventionally treated as a correctable 'soft' denial in RCM practice.
